routes.description: Establish that substantive arguments can rationally clarify and support theism despite dependence on prior commitments, then defend the actuality principle against persistence counterexamples and trace contemporaneous explanatory dependence to a purely actual divine terminus.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if detailed premise-level argument remains epistemically relevant, persistence requires positive contemporaneous actualities rather than mere noninterference, the resulting explanatory regress cannot terminate in potential or composite physical reality, and its terminus qualifies as divine.

motionBridge.description: Connect the defended Aristotelian causal reasoning to both the existence of a good argument for God and identification of its ultimate actualizer as divine.

centralBridges.description: Show that audience-relative, informal, and formally reconstructed reasoning can provide rational support without needing to compel every competent opponent.
Show that persistence and change alike depend on already actual explanatory conditions, preserving the actuality principle against the chair and universe counterexamples.
Show that contemporaneous explanatory dependence cannot terminate in anything composite or retaining unactualized potentiality, and therefore requires a purely actual terminus.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require detailed examination of particular premises and inferences instead of resolving the theistic dispute solely through abstract argument theory.
Explain why a simple terminus without parts or potentiality is not an ordinary physical constituent but bears the relevant divine status.

routes.description: Establish that premise-conclusion arguments have limited power across deep theoretical disagreement, that worldviews should instead be compared globally, and that a simpler persistence account plus an ultimate physical level blocks Feser's regress to a divine actualizer.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if Feser's proof cannot rationally move the strongest naturalist without antecedently disputed premises, persistence can occur without a distinct actualizer, or the explanatory hierarchy can terminate coherently in physical simples or fundamental physical reality rather than God.

motionBridge.description: Connect the methodological and persistence objections to the conclusion that Feser's Aristotelian proof does not establish a good argument for God.

centralBridges.description: Show that arguments principally expose consequences or inconsistency because competent opponents may rationally reject premises inherited from a rival theory.
Require global comparison of rival theories by explanatory scope and economy rather than treating a formally valid reconstruction as independently dispute-settling.
Show that successive universal states or coordinated persisting properties can be realized without a distinct already actual actualizer.
Show that constitution may bottom out in physical simples, a quantum field, or another fundamental physical level without further explanation or divinity.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Assess philosophical merit against the strongest informed rival theory rather than against sympathetic, unprepared, or already premise-accepting audiences.
Establish that the noninterference account of persistence is a genuine and comparatively simpler alternative theory rather than a verbal restatement of actualization.

sections.title: Argument Standards, Audiences, and Rational Force
sections.rationale: This issue determines what counts as a good argument, whether premise rejection limits rational force, and whether audience-relative usefulness, informal support, or formal reconstruction remains epistemically significant.

sections.title: Particular Arguments and Global Theory Comparison
sections.rationale: This issue structures whether the debate should turn on detailed scrutiny of individual proofs and disputed premises or on comparative virtues of the complete theistic and naturalistic theories.

sections.title: Actualization, Persistence, and Noninterference
sections.rationale: This is the principal direct clash over whether unchanged properties and successive states require an already actual actualizer, and therefore whether the foundational premise of the Aristotelian proof survives.

sections.title: Microstructure and Contemporaneous Explanatory Dependence
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether persisting chemical and physical structure positively explains macroscopic persistence or merely forms a coordinated state that continues without any distinct actual cause.

sections.title: Ultimate Physical Level or Purely Actual Terminus
sections.rationale: This issue governs the proof's final inference: whether explanatory descent may stop with physical simples or fundamental fields, or whether any genuine terminus must lack composition and potentiality and thus be divine.

moves.speaker: Ed Feser
moves.proposition: Theism should not be debated solely at the meta-level, because detailed examination of particular arguments is needed to expose contentious assumptions and assess their premises and inferences.
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy explicitly invites Ed to respond, and the resulting first-person turn contrasts Feser's own approach with common skeptical practice.

response.rationale: This constructive move establishes the supporting methodological requirement that particular premises and inferences receive detailed examination.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly develops its own methodological claim, though the supporting case remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposal and its qualification allowing meta-level analysis when a specific impasse arises are recoverable and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The necessity claim is confined to avoiding exclusively meta-level debate, with an express allowance for relevant meta-level disputes.

charity.alternative: Global theory comparison may remain useful even when particular arguments are also examined.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move objects to exclusive meta-level treatment rather than denying all global comparison.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The impasse example supports moving between premise-level and meta-level analysis, with one implicit bridge to general productivity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A concrete argumentative impasse supports the proposal, but no broader comparison establishes its general superiority.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the detailed-scrutiny subsidiary bridge and reaches its upper range.

representationalCharity.rationale: The position leaves room for the strongest compatible role for theory comparison and targets only exclusivity.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says discussion may move to meta-level logical disagreement when progress stops but should not remain there in theism debates.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Arguments are useful for revealing unnoticed consequences of an interlocutor's commitments, after which the interlocutor may accept the consequence or revise the underlying beliefs.
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy resumes after Feser's clarification question and develops a continuous example before explicitly stating the limited function he assigns arguments.

response.rationale: This constructive move states a central account of argument as exposing commitments while leaving belief revision open to the interlocutor.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly states and illustrates its constructive methodological thesis, though its exclusivity claim is underdefended.

precisionFindings.rationale: Commitment, logical consequence, and belief revision are distinguished clearly enough to recover the claimed function.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The assertion that this is the only useful function of argument substantially exceeds the illustrative support supplied.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between commitment and belief rationally permits either accepting a consequence or revising prior beliefs.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The example supports one useful function, but it does not warrant the universal claim that arguments have no others.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central bridge concerning argument limits and states that bridge in unusually explicit terms.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move advances its own general account without materially interpreting a developed opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes being committed to a consequence from believing it, permits revising beliefs, and calls consequence revelation argument's only use.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Competing worldviews should be compared globally by theoretical virtues, including explanatory breadth and economy, while arguments play the narrower preliminary role of exposing inconsistency.
moves.attributionBasis: Oppy explicitly returns to his original thesis and lays out theory comparison, global virtues, articulation, consistency checking, and argument's role.

components.text: Whether detailed scrutiny of particular premises and inferences should remain methodologically important.

response.rationale: The move directly counters the methodological demand by proposing global comparison through explanatory breadth and economy, although it does not show that local scrutiny lacks value.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive methodological component but only partially answers why detailed scrutiny should be displaced.

precisionFindings.rationale: Global comparison and theoretical virtues are clear, while the reduced role assigned to argument carries an implicit rather than stated scope limit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The proposed comparison is plausible, but the limited role for argument is not fully derived from the named virtues.

charity.alternative: Detailed premise scrutiny can contribute to an eventual global comparison rather than compete with it.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move does not establish that global virtues eliminate the local evidential role of particular arguments.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The theory-choice proposal is intelligible, but the inference from global virtues to little role for argument leaves a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Explanatory breadth and economy are relevant criteria, yet their priority and the exclusionary conclusion remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It expressly supplies the global theory-comparison central bridge and articulates its governing criteria.

representationalCharity.rationale: It recognizes theory-level assessment but gives insufficient attention to the strongest complementary account of local scrutiny.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies minimizing commitments and maximizing explanatory breadth as theory-choice criteria and says global weighing leaves little role for argument.

moves.speaker: Ed Feser
moves.proposition: An argument's rational force and practical usefulness vary with an audience's prior commitments, knowledge, and susceptibility to its premises, even when the argument does not compel every informed opponent.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn is a sustained first-person response using Mackie and Churchland examples characteristic of Feser's defense of arguments against Oppy's restriction.

components.text: Whether revealing unnoticed consequences exhausts the rationally useful functions of argument.
Whether arguments retain epistemic value when global theoretical comparison is also relevant.

response.rationale: The move diagnoses the exclusivity claim as overlooking audience-relative variation and states the defeating consequence that arguments can rationally persuade some listeners without compelling all.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive exclusivity premise and explains why audience variation defeats it.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The audience-relative conclusion is proportionate to the examples and expressly allows resistant audiences to reject crucial premises.

charity.alternative: The strongest informed opponent may rationally reject premises despite other audiences finding them persuasive.
charity.decisiveQualification: Failure to compel that opponent does not show that consequence revelation is the argument's only rational use.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Mackie-style audience example is specific and apt, though broader representativeness remains an implicit warrant.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly and strongly supplies the central argumentative-relevance bridge at the top of its tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move preserves the opponent's premise-rejection point while accurately challenging its universal methodological consequence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt places arguments on a spectrum determined largely by the listener and notes that many theists would reject Mackie's crucial premises.

moves.speaker: Ed Feser
moves.proposition: Formal reconstruction can clarify the basic structure of an extended line of reasoning and assist audiences receptive to its premises, even though the reconstruction cannot by itself settle the dispute.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker identifies his own Five Proofs and Aristotelian proof, explains its chapter structure, and explicitly states his partial agreement and disagreement with Oppy.

Whether argument has rational uses beyond revealing contradictions or unnoticed consequences.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: Philosophical disputes are more productively addressed by comparing disputed claims and their supporting theories than by concentrating on the formal properties of particular arguments.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn directly follows a question addressed to Graham and develops Oppy's previously stated account of theories, claims, and arguments.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The productivity claim is plausible but lacks an explicit condition explaining when formal properties cease to matter.

moves.speaker: Ed Feser
moves.proposition: Given the shared analysis of change as the actualization of potential, a noninterference account of persistence does not supply a genuine alternative to the requirement for an already actual actualizer.
moves.attributionBasis: Feser introduces the passage as his response to Graham's red-chair counterexample and repeatedly contrasts Graham's principle with his own principle.

components.text: Whether the proposed rival principle constitutes a genuinely distinct and preferable theoretical alternative.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies the alleged failure and consequence, although the decisive equivalence warrant remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is explicitly conditional on accepting change as actualization of potential and clearly identifies the alleged equivalence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Although the shared-analysis condition is stated, the certainty that noninterference is a restatement outruns the supplied demonstration.

charity.alternative: Noninterference may describe persistence without positing a positive actualizing condition.
charity.decisiveQualification: Shared language about potentials alone does not establish that noninterference and positive actualization are equivalent.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move identifies the rival view but materially understates its claim to omit a distinct positive actualizer.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt conditions its response on change as actualization of potential and repeatedly says Oppy's alternative amounts to Feser's own principle.

moves.speaker: Ed Feser
moves.proposition: The Aristotelian premise requires every actualized potential to have an already actual actualizer, but it does not require that actualizer to be wholly external to the changing thing.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly corrects how his own argument's premise was formulated and illustrates the correction through his present bodily movement.

components.text: What precise substantive causal principle is actually disputed rather than merely its informal formulation.

response.rationale: The move justifies replacing the vague external-changer formulation with the already-actual actualizer principle, preserving the causal issue while removing an ambiguity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly identifies the ambiguity, states the replacement demand, and explains why the technical formulation is required.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move precisely distinguishes an external changer from something already actual and explicitly confines its correction.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move states the principle being defended rather than claiming to have independently established its truth in this span.

charity.alternative: The objection may target external causation rather than every form of already-actual actualization.
charity.decisiveQualification: Feser's stated premise does not require the actualizer to be wholly external to the changing thing.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The ambiguity diagnosis and corrected formulation are explicit, consistent, and directly resolve the formulation challenge.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt rejects the vague claim that change requires an external changer and formulates the premise as actualized potential requiring something already actual.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: The universe can possess a potential for a later state without anything already actual actualizing that potential, directly denying the proposed universal actuality principle.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker accepts Feser's reformulation for discussion, then explicitly states disagreement with its requirement when applied to the universe.

components.text: Whether every actualized potential requires something already actual to actualize it.

response.rationale: The move directly denies the corrected universal principle through a universe-state counterexample, but it asserts the countermodel rather than explaining how realization occurs.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive universal premise and gives a directly relevant counterexample.

precisionFindings.rationale: The universe, its later-state potential, and denial of an already-actual actualizer are stated without material ambiguity.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A bare assertion that the universe can realize the potential does not yet warrant categorical rejection of the universal principle.

charity.alternative: An already-actual condition within or grounding the universe could account for the later state.
charity.decisiveQualification: The principle does not require an actualizer external to the universe.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample would refute the universal premise if possible, but its central possibility is asserted without a usable realization account.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The universe example supplies no mechanism or independent warrant showing potential realization without any already-actual condition.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central actualization bridge by categorically denying its universal principle.

representationalCharity.rationale: The counterexample targets the universal claim but omits the decisive qualification that the actualizer need not be external.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt recasts the example in potentiality terms and says the universe's potential for a later state needs no already-actual actualizer.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: A red chair's potential to remain red at the next moment is realized by default when nothing intervenes, so persistence does not require a distinct actualizer.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker reconstructs the chair example from his own disputed formulation and closes by denying the need for the actualizer Feser posits.

components.text: Whether persistence of an instantiated property counts as actualization requiring an already-actual actualizer.
Whether noninterference is genuinely distinct from the actuality principle.

response.rationale: The move supplies a distinct default-persistence model in which redness remains unless an intervention realizes another potential, directly contesting both the universal premise and equivalence claim.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly contacts both decisive demands and states a concrete rival account of the chair case.

precisionFindings.rationale: The chair's current redness, next-moment redness, alternative potentials, and intervention condition are clearly distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The countermodel is clearly specified, but the claim that persistence requires no actualizer remains stronger than its descriptive setup alone warrants.

charity.alternative: Persisting microstructure could be a positive contemporaneous explanatory actuality rather than mere absence of interference.
charity.decisiveQualification: A complete rival must distinguish the default condition from the physical grounds enabling continued redness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The default-persistence account is coherent, though the inference from no disrupting event to no positive actualizer leaves one material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The paintball example illustrates intervention clearly but does not establish that noninterference exhausts the explanatory conditions.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central persistence-countermodel bridge with the debate's principal concrete example.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move gives a genuine rival model but does not yet address the strongest contemporaneous-ground interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts paintball-driven alternative potentials with the chair's potential to remain red and denies that persistence requires another actualizer.

moves.speaker: Ed Feser
moves.proposition: A chair's continued redness depends on molecular and atomic organization existing at that same moment, providing contemporaneous explanatory actualities and initiating the regress toward a purely actual actualizer.
moves.attributionBasis: The response invokes the purely actual actualizer terminology of Feser's argument and defends the actuality principle against the chair example.

components.text: Whether absence of intervention is a sufficient explanation of the chair's continued redness.
Whether a later actual state can occur without contemporaneous already-actual explanatory conditions.

response.rationale: The move diagnoses noninterference as omitting same-moment molecular and atomic conditions and states that these positive actualities reopen the explanatory regress.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies the omitted explanatory component and states its consequence for the actuality principle and regress.

precisionFindings.rationale: Same-moment explanatory dependence is distinguished from earlier temporal causes, and the regress claim is expressly identified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Microstructural dependence is plausibly necessary for redness, but moving from dependence to the relevant actualizing causality is compressed.

charity.alternative: Microstructure and redness may persist together under one coordinated default condition.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Molecular and atomic organization provide a specific explanatory basis, though the metaphysical causal interpretation is underdefended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central actualization bridge by identifying positive contemporaneous explanatory actualities.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately preserves the strongest default-persistence option while identifying its unresolved explanatory demand.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt isolates conditions existing when the chair is red and says this contemporaneous causality generates the regress toward a purely actual actualizer.

moves.speaker: Graham Oppy
moves.proposition: The chair's redness and underlying physical properties can persist together unless an intervention produces connected changes, so its microstructure need not serve as a distinct actualizer.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage directly answers Feser's chemical-structure explanation from Oppy's previously stated persistence framework.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says paint changes both surface reflectance and redness, while absent chemical change both persist as connected properties.

moves.speaker: Ed Feser
moves.proposition: Continued redness is not explained merely by the absence of interference, because the macroscopic property contemporaneously depends on the chair's persisting chemical microstructure.
moves.attributionBasis: The response restates Feser's premise and is followed by the moderator explicitly asking Graham for his counterexample.

components.text: Whether coordinated persistence removes the need for a positive contemporaneous explanation of redness.
